author: John Chrysostom
occasion: Two catechetical homilies (Πρώτη and Δευτέρα) delivered to those about to be baptized (φωτίζεσθαι), covering baptismal preparation, moral purification, and renunciation of Satan.
argument: Chrysostom first celebrates the catechumens' decision and contrasts their deliberate preparation with deathbed baptism. He explains the many names of baptism, especially 'washing of regeneration', showing that it does not merely forgive sins but recreates the whole person. He then urges them to master the tongue, above all by renouncing all oaths, and to reform their habits before baptism. In the second instruction he warns against luxury, especially women's jewelry, and against pagan practices such as omens, amulets, and incantations, urging them to make the baptismal renunciation of Satan their daily weapon.

outline.move: Chrysostom greets the candidates, praises their early zeal, and asks them to remember him when they enter the heavenly kingdom.
He contrasts their willing, joyful preparation with the distress and confusion of deathbed baptism.
He introduces the many names of baptism and begins to explain why it is called the washing of regeneration.
He shows that baptism cleanses real moral defilement, not merely ritual impurity, and makes sinners holy and righteous.
He develops the image of God melting down and recasting human nature like a gold statue or potter's vessel.
He compares the thirty days before baptism to athletic training and warns that the tongue is the devil's chief weapon.
He urges them to guard the tongue and imposes one law: avoid all oaths, even truthful ones.
He insists that no one's rank excuses oath-taking and advises enlisting family and friends as guardians.
He proposes a ten-day trial period with self-imposed penalties for anyone who swears.
He explains the name 'human being' (ἄνθρωπος) as defined by virtue and piety, and 'faithful' (πιστός) as one who trusts God and receives from him righteousness, holiness, and adoption.

He describes how baptismal grace dispels fear of death, poverty, and sickness by teaching that death is temporary sleep, and shows how Christ becomes everything to the believer—garment, table, house, head, root, brother, friend, bridegroom.
He warns them to keep the baptismal garment unstained and to correct their habits before baptism.
He teaches that no one can harm the soul of a Christian and that no external condition prevents virtue.

He contrasts God's merciful enlistment with earthly military and theatrical recruitment: God accepts slaves, elderly, and disabled, makes sinners his allies rather than exposing their crimes, and fights alongside them.
He urges artisans and the poor to practice virtue and psalmody in their workshops, and praises poverty.
He addresses women, urging them to adorn themselves with virtue rather than pearls and gold.
He explains the renunciation of Satan as a voluntary covenant with Christ (contrasted with slave purchase), and condemns omens, day-observance, and symbols as Satanic pomp.
He attacks amulets, incantations, and Alexander coins, and urges the sign of the cross and the renunciation formula as daily armor.

key_terms.sense: To be enlightened, i.e. to receive baptism.
The washing of regeneration, baptism as a complete re-creation.
Initiation into the sacred mysteries, i.e. baptism.
The sacred rites, especially baptism and the Eucharist.

candidates: I turn away from you, Satan

key_terms.sense: The devil's pageantry: theaters, races, omens, amulets, and all sin.
The covenant or agreement made with Christ at baptism.
A deposit entrusted to someone; here the faith and grace entrusted by God and the renunciation entrusted by the believer.
Oaths of any kind, which Chrysostom forbids entirely.
Keeping an oath, swearing truthfully; still forbidden.
Omens or chance utterances interpreted as signs.
Chance encounters treated as omens, e.g. meeting a one-eyed man.
Incantations or spells, often using God's name.

scripture: Chrysostom quotes the Septuagint and follows its book names and Psalm numbering. In translation, use standard English Bible names and Hebrew Psalm numbering where they differ from the LXX, with a note when the LXX numbering is one behind the Hebrew.
uncertain: The exact date of delivery; c. 388–390 is probable but not certain.
The precise identity of the 'one who said' the proverbs about the tongue in section 6; likely Sirach, but Chrysostom does not name him.
Whether the two catecheses were delivered in the same year or in successive years.
